meta.title: Who really said "Military Command: Send Three and Fourpence. We're Going to a Dance"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No officer, unit or date was ever named. Earliest printing: a London periodical, 15 October 1914; the 'dance' wording by 1916. A joke, not a real WWI signal.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Military Command: Send Three and Fourpence. We're Going to a Dance'?
meta.ogDescription: A famous 'garbled WWI message' with no sender, no unit and no date - first printed as a joke in 1914, and retold as a Second World War story by 1943.

answer.label: Not a genuine First World War signal — an anonymous joke
answer.sourceLine: No sender, unit, date or receiving headquarters has ever been attached to this message. The earliest printing anyone has located is an unsigned filler item headed “Altered in Transit” in the London periodical The Temperance Caterer of 15 October 1914 — where the garbled punchline is “ham-shanks,” not a dance — and the familiar dance-and-fourpence pairing surfaces in a New Zealand newspaper in February 1916. Quote Investigator, which traced the whole family of retellings from 1914 to 1943, allows that some relay exercise may lie underneath, but concludes that “the cleverness of many of these anecdotes suggests fabrication.”

source.heading: Where it actually comes from

docMeta.dd: “Altered in Transit,” The Temperance Caterer (London), 15 October 1914, p. 78
Harold Baldwin, Holding the Line (Chicago: A. C. McClurg, 1918), p. 128
Anonymous — no named sender, unit, date or headquarters in any known source

source.excerpt: One of the methods of communicating from one officer to another in the trenches of the present great war is to give the message to one of the privates and tell him to pass the word along the line until it reached its destination… Lieutenant A., in charge of one end of the British line told the private in front to pass the word along to Lieutenant B.: “We are going to advance, can you send us reinforcements?” When Lieutenant B. received the message it was like this: “We are going to a dance, can you lend us three and fourpence?”
trail: 15 October 1914 — London. The earliest printing found is a filler item headed “Altered in Transit” in The Temperance Caterer: a brigadier on manoeuvres at Aldershot passes “Enemy advancing from the left flank. Send reinforcements,” and the far end of the line receives “Enemy advancing with ham-shanks. Send three and fourpence!” Quote Investigator ↗

22 February 1916 — New Zealand. The two halves of the modern line finally appear together, in the Marlborough Express ↗ of Blenheim, and the setting has moved from a parade ground to the trenches: “We are going to a dance, can you lend us three and fourpence?”

1918 — a memoir, in hard covers. Sergeant Harold Baldwin of the 1st Division, Canadian Expeditionary Force, tells it as non-fiction from his own runner training: the message left as “Am held up by barbed wire entanglements; send reinforcements to my right” and arrived as “Am surrounded by wild Italians; lend me three- and fourpence till to-night.” Holding the Line, p. 128 ↗

1925–1943 — the joke keeps travelling. A syndicated humour column has Colonel Lang’s trousers sent out to be pressed in July 1925; Boys’ Life converts the sum to “three or four cents” in April 1938; and by March 1943 a CBS correspondent is telling it from Cairo as a Second World War story. the later citations ↗
source.excerptNote: The earliest pairing of “a dance” with “three and fourpence” that Quote Investigator located, transcribed from the Marlborough Express of 22 February 1916. Note what is missing: the officers are “Lieutenant A.” and “Lieutenant B.,” there is no unit, and there is no date of the supposed incident.

artifact.linkText: Harold Baldwin, Holding the Line, page 128

source.rightsNote: There is no identifiable author or work to attach rights to. The wording is an anonymous joke that mutated across newspapers, magazines and broadcasts, and the tidy modern one-liner matches none of the documented period texts exactly. The individual early printings quoted here — the 1914 Temperance Caterer filler, the 1916 Marlborough Express note and Harold Baldwin’s Holding the Line (1918) — were all published well before 1931 and are out of copyright in the United States, but that says nothing about the catchphrase itself, whose origin is unknown.

author.name: Anonymous
author.heading: So who did say it?
author.metaLine: Unattributed · British military humour, first printed 15 October 1914
author.bio: Nobody has ever been named — not the officer who sent it, not the headquarters that received it, not the wit who invented it. The line belongs to the class of jokes newspapers printed as filler about the New Armies of 1914–18, passed on as fact and reshaped by whoever was telling it. That is why the punchline is ham-shanks in a London paper in 1914, a dance in New Zealand in 1916, and wild Italians in a Canadian sergeant’s memoir in 1918.

misattribution.heading: What’s wrong with the story as told
misattribution.intro: It is almost always presented as a real signal — an officer in the line asking for reinforcements, a headquarters receiving a request for pocket money. Four things in that telling do not survive contact with the sources.

items.who: A genuine First World War signal
items.why: No sender, unit, date or receiving headquarters has ever been produced. What survives is a chain of newspaper and magazine retellings whose details change every time. Quote Investigator, having traced them from 1914 to 1943, allows there may be some founding incident but concludes that “the cleverness of many of these anecdotes suggests fabrication” and that some variants were consciously built by altering earlier ones. Quote Investigator ↗

The 1914 original pairs “Send reinforcements” with “Enemy advancing with ham-shanks. Send three and fourpence!” The dance appears in 1916 as “We are going to a dance, can you lend us three and fourpence?” The symmetrical one-liner in circulation today matches neither exactly. the documented texts ↗

items.who: Aldershot, Salisbury, the trenches, a Canadian training field, a Scout camp
items.why: Every retelling relocates it: brigade manoeuvres at Aldershot in 1914; “Kipling’s million” drilling at Salisbury in the Boston Globe of 6 January 1915; the trenches by February 1916; a Canadian runner relay in 1918; an American message-passing game in Boys’ Life in 1938. A story that fits everywhere fits nowhere in particular. the chronology ↗

By 28 March 1943 the Pittsburgh Press was reporting a CBS broadcast from Cairo in which the same exchange is told as a story of that war, with a colonel demanding to know what all this is about a dance. Quote Investigator ↗

Those words are a research headline, not part of any period text — they head Quote Investigator’s write-up, which is titled “Quote Origin: Military Command: Send Three and Fourpence. We’re Going to a Dance.” None of the 1914–1943 sources quoted there frames the line that way. the article ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The oldest thing anybody has found is an unsigned joke in a London periodical of 15 October 1914 — and even there the punchline is ham-shanks, not a dance. Quote Investigator, 26 August 2011 ↗

context.heading: Why a joke this old refuses to die
lead: The gag lands because the problem underneath it was real. When telephone cable was cut by shellfire — as it was at the Battle of Neuve-Chapelle ↗ on 10–13 March 1915, where the British telephone system proved vulnerable to German artillery-fire — a message had to travel by human relay, and every relay is a fresh chance to mishear. Sergeant Harold Baldwin, who tells one of the earliest versions, explains in the same breath that company runners were formed after Neuve Chapelle ↗ precisely because that engagement had shown what happens when the wires go.

So the anecdote never had to be true to be useful, and that is exactly what has kept it alive: it is the cleanest one-sentence demonstration of message decay anybody has ever come up with. It has been repurposed as a training-room parable, a management column opener and an after-dinner line for more than a century — usually with an air of documentary certainty that the actual paper trail does not support.
detailsBody: The two halves of the modern couplet arrive separately. “Send three and fourpence” is present from the very first printing in 1914, where it answers a request for reinforcements against an enemy advancing “with ham-shanks.” The dance only joins it in 1916. The neat symmetry everyone quotes — advance/a dance, reinforcements/three and fourpence — is a later polish, not the original.

The currency dates it and localises it. Three shillings and fourpence only scans as a sum of money in pre-decimal Britain, which is why American retellings had to translate: Boys’ Life was asking for “three or four cents” by April 1938.

sourcesVerified.claim: The earliest version located is “Altered in Transit,” The Temperance Caterer (London), 15 October 1914, p. 78, with “Enemy advancing with ham-shanks. Send three and fourpence!”; the dance pairing appears in the Marlborough Express (NZ) of 22 February 1916, p. 5; Harold Baldwin's Holding the Line (1918) p. 128 carries the “wild Italians” variant; the Boston Globe (6 Jan 1915) sets it at Salisbury; a 1925 syndicated column has Col. Lang's pants pressed; Boys' Life (April 1938, p. 47) uses “three or four cents”; the Pittsburgh Press of 28 March 1943 reports a CBS broadcast from Cairo relocating it to WWII; QI concludes “the cleverness of many of these anecdotes suggests fabrication.” The article is titled “Quote Origin: Military Command: Send Three and Fourpence. We're Going to a Dance.”

Page 128 of Harold Baldwin's Holding the Line reads: the first man was given “To O. C. Seventh Battalion: Am held up by barbed wire entanglements; send reinforcements to my right,” and the officer received “Am surrounded by wild Italians; lend me three- and fourpence till to-night.” Page 127 states that company runners “were formed after Neuve Chapelle. In that engagement disastrous results followed the cutting of all telephone communication.”
Bibliographic record: “Holding the line,” by Baldwin, Harold; publisher A. C. McClurg; Chicago; 1918.
The Marlborough Express is a New Zealand newspaper headquartered in Blenheim, established 1866 and published daily from 1880, so it was publishing in 1916.
Wikipedia's article on Chinese whispers describes the message-distortion game (the “telephone” game) but does NOT mention the “send three and fourpence / going to a dance” anecdote.

The Battle of Neuve-Chapelle took place 10–13 March 1915, and the article states that the British telephone system proved vulnerable to German artillery-fire, with command undermined by communication failures.

This Google Books volume is the April 1938 issue of Boys' Life, published by the Boy Scouts of America — the issue Quote Investigator cites for the “three or four cents” retelling. (The issue identity was confirmed; the page-47 text itself was not visible in the fetched view.)
